# 13 An introduction to AS Level organic chemistry

本章只覆盖 AS 3.1：有机物的表示法、同系物与官能团、命名、反应类型与试剂角色、σ/π 键和杂化，以及结构异构与立体异构。下方题目均来自 **3.1 An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry** 的 AS 原题；无法独立提取的题图没有以截图方式加入。

## Learning objectives

- use molecular, empirical, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae correctly;
- identify functional groups, homologous series and structural isomerism;
- apply IUPAC naming rules to simple aliphatic compounds;
- distinguish electrophiles, nucleophiles and free radicals, and name the mechanism/reaction type;
- explain σ and π bonds, hybridisation and molecular shape;
- distinguish E/Z (cis-trans) and optical isomerism.

## 13.1 Formulas, Functional Groups - the Naming of Organic Compounds

A **molecular formula** gives the actual number of each atom, for example C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O. An **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio, so the empirical formula of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O is also C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, but that of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> is CH<sub>2</sub>O. A **structural formula** groups atoms along the chain, a **displayed formula** shows every bond, and a **skeletal formula** uses line ends/vertices for carbon atoms and omits C-bound H atoms. Hydrogen attached to a heteroatom, for example the O–H hydrogen in an alcohol, is shown.

A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula. Consecutive members differ by CH<sub>2</sub>; they have similar chemical properties but show a gradual change in physical properties. A **hydrocarbon** contains hydrogen and carbon only. Important AS patterns are:

| Homologous series | Functional group / general formula | Example suffix |
|---|---|---|
| alkane | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, C–C only | -ane |
| alkene | C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, C=C | -ene |
| halogenoalkane | C–X | fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo- |
| alcohol | –OH | -ol |
| aldehyde | –CHO | -al |
| ketone | >C=O | -one |
| carboxylic acid | –COOH | -oic acid |
| ester | –COO– | alkyl alkanoate |
| nitrile | –C≡N | -nitrile |

![Functional groups in important AS organic families](../assets/notes/organic-as-13-rebuilt/formulas-img-010.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Functional groups in important AS organic families"}

### Naming organic compounds

Choose the longest carbon chain containing the highest-priority functional group. Number it from the end that gives the functional group the lowest possible number, then give substituents their locants and list them alphabetically. The stem tells the number of C atoms: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-. Include a number before -ene, -ol or -one when its position is not fixed.

For example, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is **butan-2-ol**, and CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Br)CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>OH is **3-bromo-2-methylbutan-1-ol**. In a carboxylic acid the carboxyl carbon is carbon 1 by definition. In an aldehyde, the –CHO carbon is carbon 1 and its hydrogen must not be omitted from a displayed formula.

## 13.2 Characteristic Organic Reactions

Organic reactions can be described both by reaction type and by mechanism. **Addition** joins atoms to a molecule (often across C=C); **substitution** replaces one atom/group by another; **elimination** removes a small molecule to form a multiple bond; **hydrolysis** breaks a bond using water; **oxidation** raises the oxidation state / adds oxygen / removes hydrogen.

An **electrophile** accepts an electron pair and attacks an electron-rich region, such as the π bond of an alkene. A **nucleophile** donates an electron pair; OH<sup>−</sup>, CN<sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub> are common examples. A **free radical** has an unpaired electron and is shown with a dot, for example Cl·.

Bond fission is central to mechanisms:

- **Homolytic fission:** one electron goes to each atom, forming radicals: Cl–Cl → 2Cl·.
- **Heterolytic fission:** both bonding electrons go to one atom, forming ions: C–Br → C<sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>−</sup> (direction depends on relative electronegativity).

Free-radical substitution of an alkane with chlorine under UV light has three stages: **initiation** (Cl–Cl → 2Cl·), **propagation** (radicals react and a new radical is regenerated), and **termination** (two radicals combine). Electrophilic addition occurs when an electrophile accepts the π electrons of an alkene; nucleophilic substitution occurs when a nucleophile replaces a leaving group such as Br<sup>−</sup> in a halogenoalkane.

![Addition, substitution and elimination reactions](../assets/notes/organic-as-13-rebuilt/reactions-img-040.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Examples of addition, substitution and elimination reactions"}

## 13.3 Shapes of Organic Molecules; σ - π Bonds

A single bond is one **σ bond**, made by end-on overlap. A double bond contains one σ bond and one **π bond**; a triple bond contains one σ bond and two π bonds. A π bond is made by sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals and prevents free rotation about the double bond. This restricted rotation is required for E/Z (cis-trans) isomerism.

| Hybridisation at carbon | Typical bonding | Shape and approximate angle |
|---|---|---|
| sp<sup>3</sup> | four σ bonds | tetrahedral, 109.5° |
| sp<sup>2</sup> | three σ bonds + one unhybridised p orbital | trigonal planar, 120° |
| sp | two σ bonds + two unhybridised p orbitals | linear, 180° |

Thus each carbon of C=C is sp<sup>2</sup> and trigonal planar. In C≡C each carbon is sp and linear. In methane, one 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals, which repel to a tetrahedral arrangement. Cyclohexane is not planar: sp<sup>3</sup> carbon favours angles close to 109.5°, and a puckered conformation reduces strain.

![σ and π bonding in ethene](../assets/notes/organic-as-13-rebuilt/shapes-img-024.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Sigma and pi bonding in ethene"}

## 13.4 Isomerism. Structural Isomerism - Stereoisomerism

**Structural isomers** have the same molecular formula but different connectivity. The three types are **chain isomerism** (different carbon skeleton), **positional isomerism** (same functional group in a different position) and **functional-group isomerism** (different functional groups).

**Stereoisomers** have the same connectivity but different arrangement in space. E/Z (cis-trans) isomerism requires restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups attached to each carbon of the double bond. A **chiral centre** is usually a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups. A chiral molecule can form a pair of non-superimposable mirror images called **enantiomers**; this is optical isomerism. A molecule with an internal plane of symmetry is not chiral.

![Geometric isomerism caused by restricted rotation](../assets/notes/organic-as-13-rebuilt/isomerism-img-060.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Cis-trans isomerism in alkenes and rings"}

::: {.mc-question #aso-mc-01 data-answer="B"}
### Question 1 · 3.1 Choice Easy Q1
<p>Which pairs of homologous series do not have the same C:H ratio in their general formulae?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>Aldehydes and ketones</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>Alkanes and alkenes</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>Carboxylic acids and esters</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>Alkenes and aldehydes</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>B.</strong> Alkanes have C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, whereas alkenes have C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #aso-mc-02 data-answer="C"}
### Question 2 · 3.1 Choice Easy Q2
<p>The disaccharide sucrose, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>, is found in biscuits and cakes. Inside the body, sucrose is hydrolysed to produce glucose and fructose. Which statements about the hydrolysis products are correct?<br>1. Glucose and fructose have structural isomers.<br>2. Glucose and fructose are ketones.<br>3. Glucose is a carboxylic acid.<br>4. Glucose and fructose have optical isomers.</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>1 and 2</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>2 and 4</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>1 and 4</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>1, 2 and 4</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>C.</strong> Glucose and fructose are structural isomers and each has chiral centres, so optical isomers are possible; the other statements are false.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #aso-mc-03 data-answer="B"}

### Question 7 · 3.1 Choice Medium Q1
<p>Evening primrose oil has been shown to reduce high blood pressure and improve heart health. The oil is made from seeds, within which the active compound gamma-linolenic acid is found. How many stereoisomers does gamma-linolenic acid have?</p>
![Displayed formula of gamma-linolenic acid](../assets/questions/extracted/13/rebuilt/choice-medium-q1-gamma-linolenic-acid.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Displayed formula of gamma-linolenic acid"}
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>6</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>8</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>4</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>C.</strong> The molecule has three independent C=C bonds capable of E/Z isomerism, giving 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 stereoisomers.</li></ul></details>

<p>Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits. How many σ and π bonds are present in this molecule?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>24 σ and 4 π</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>12 σ and 2 π</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>26 σ and 2 π</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>22 σ and 4 π</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>C.</strong> There are 26 σ bonds and 2 π bonds; each double bond contributes one σ and one π bond.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #aso-mc-19 data-answer="C"}
### Question 19 · 3.1 Choice Hard Q8
<p>Including structural and stereoisomers, how many isomeric products are produced when alcoholic NaOH reacts with 2-bromobutane?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>1</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>2</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>4</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>C.</strong> Elimination gives but-1-ene and but-2-ene; but-2-ene has cis and trans forms, giving three products.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #aso-mc-20 data-answer="D"}
### Question 20 · 3.1 Choice Hard Q9
<p>How many isomers, including structural and stereoisomers, with the formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> have structures that involve π bonding?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>4</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>5</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>6</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback" aria-live="polite"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><ul><li><strong>D.</strong> Counting the alkene structures and the E/Z stereoisomers separately gives six.</li></ul></details>
:::

## Structured questions

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-01}
### Question 1 · 3.1 SQ Easy Q1(a-e)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Propane and hexane are part of the alkane homologous series.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Define the term hydrocarbon.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Give the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(iii)</strong> State the formula of an alkane containing five carbon atoms.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State three characteristics of a homologous series.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Give the IUPAC names for the following aliphatic molecules.</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Molecule</th><th>Name</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>CH<sub>3</sub>CH(Cl)CH<sub>3</sub></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH</td><td></td></tr><tr><td>CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(Br)CH<sub>2</sub>OH</td><td></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> The structures of four organic compounds are shown in Fig. 1.1. Complete Table 1.2 by naming the organic compounds and their functional groups.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> The compound 2,2-dimethylpentan-3-ol can be represented using different types of formulae. Its structural formula can be shown as C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(e)(i)</strong> Give the empirical formula of 2,2-dimethylpentan-3-ol.</p>
<p><strong>(e)(ii)</strong> Draw the skeletal formula of 2,2-dimethylpentan-3-ol.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)(i)</strong> A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen only.</li><li><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>.</li><li><strong>(a)(iii)</strong> C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Any three: the same functional group; the same general formula; adjacent members differ by CH<sub>2</sub>; similar chemical properties; gradual changes in physical properties.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> 2-chloropropane; but-1-ene; propan-1-ol; 2-bromo-1-hydroxybutane.</li><li><strong>(e)(i)</strong> C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O.</li><li><strong>(e)(ii)</strong> A correctly connected skeletal formula with a six-carbon chain, a methyl branch at C2 and OH at C3.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-02}
### Question 2 · 3.1 SQ Easy Q2(a-c)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> State the three different types of structural isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State the type of isomerism that occurs between the following pairs of compounds.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> 2-methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Compounds A to F are shown in Fig. 2.1.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> State the IUPAC name for compound B.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> State the type of structural isomerism that occurs between compounds A and D.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(iii)</strong> State the type of structural isomerism that occurs between compounds C and E.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Chain isomerism, positional isomerism and functional-group isomerism.</li><li><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Chain isomerism.</li><li><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Positional isomerism.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Compound B: butanal. A and D: positional isomerism. C and E: functional-group isomerism.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-03}
### Question 3 · 3.1 SQ Easy Q3(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Free radical substitution reactions involve hydrogen atoms in alkanes being replaced by halogen atoms. Name the three steps involved in a free radical substitution reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> When a molecule of chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>, is exposed to UV light two chlorine radicals are formed.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Write an equation for this reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> State the type of bond fission involved.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Fig. 3.1 shows the breaking of a covalent bond, where the more electronegative atom B has taken both electrons from the bond to form a negative ion. State the name of this type of bond fission.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Name three other types of reaction mechanism.</p>
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/13/rebuilt/sq-easy-q3c-heterolytic-fission.png" class="question-figure" alt="Heterolytic bond fission showing both bonding electrons moving to atom B">
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Initiation, propagation and termination.</li><li><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl· under UV light.</li><li><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Homolytic fission.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Heterolytic fission.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> Any three: free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution, nucleophilic addition or electrophilic substitution.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-04}
### Question 4 · 3.1 SQ Easy Q4(a-c)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Aliphatic compounds can be organised into three different categories depending on their structure. One of the categories is straight-chain. Name the other two categories of aliphatic compounds.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Complete Table 4.1 to show the type and number of bonds in hybridised bonds.</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Hybridisation</th><th>Number of σ bonds</th><th>Number of π bonds</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>sp<sup>3</sup></td><td></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>sp<sup>2</sup></td><td></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>sp</td><td></td><td></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Four compounds are shown in Fig. 4.1. Complete Table 4.2 to name the shapes and bond angles of the four planar molecules.</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Molecule</th><th>Shape</th><th>Bond angle /°</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Carbon dioxide</td><td>Linear</td><td></td></tr><tr><td>Water</td><td></td><td>104.5</td></tr><tr><td>Boron trifluoride</td><td></td><td>120</td></tr><tr><td>Cisplatin</td><td>Square planar</td><td></td></tr></tbody></table>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Branched-chain and cyclic.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> sp<sup>3</sup>: 4 σ, 0 π; sp<sup>2</sup>: 3 σ, 1 π; sp: 2 σ, 2 π.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Carbon dioxide: linear, 180°. Water: bent, 104.5°. Boron trifluoride: trigonal planar, 120°. Cisplatin: square planar, 90°.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-05}
### Question 5 · 3.1 SQ Easy Q5(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Name the two types of stereoisomers.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Describe what a chiral centre is.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> The structure of one optical isomer of a chlorofluorocarbon is shown in Fig. 5.1. Draw the structure of the other enantiomer.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> The skeletal structure of a halogenoalkane is shown in Fig. 5.2. Explain why the carbon labelled a cannot be a chiral centre.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Optical isomers and geometrical isomers.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> A tetrahedral carbon atom attached to four different atoms or groups.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Draw the non-superimposable mirror image of the given structure.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> Carbon a is attached to two identical groups, so it does not have four different substituents.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-06}
### Question 6 · 3.1 SQ Medium Q1(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> A chemist is analysing a collection of organic compounds. Some of these compounds are shown in Table 1.1. Complete Table 1.1.</p>
<table><thead><tr><th>Compound</th><th>IUPAC name</th><th>Displayed formula</th><th>Skeletal formula</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1</td><td>Z-2-chlorobut-2-en-1-ol</td><td></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>2-chloropropanal</td><td></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr><tr><td>4</td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State the empirical formula of compound 1.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Explain why compound 1 exists as two stereoisomers, but compound 4 does not.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Compounds 2 and 3 both exhibit the same type of isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> State the type of isomerism shown by compounds 2 and 3.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> Draw the two isomers of compound 2 to explain how this type of isomerism occurs.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Complete the displayed and skeletal formulae using the stated IUPAC names and the structures shown in the source table.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ClO.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Compound 1 has restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups on each alkene carbon, whereas compound 4 lacks the required pair of different substituents.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> Geometrical (E/Z) isomerism; draw the two arrangements around the C=C bond.</li></ul></details>

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-07}
### Question 7 · 3.1 SQ Medium Q2(a-c)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Explain how the concept of hybridisation can be used to explain the triple bond present in propyne.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Consider the molecule shown in Fig. 2.1 which contains both sigma and pi bonds. State the number of carbon atoms that exhibit sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation in this molecule.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Complete Table 2.1 to show the hybridisation of the nitrogen atoms in NF<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Each C in C≡C is sp hybridised; one sp orbital from each C forms the σ bond and two unhybridised p orbitals on each C form two perpendicular π bonds. The bond angle is 180°.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Count the carbon atoms with three electron-density regions around them, including each C in a C=C bond.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> NF<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>: sp<sup>3</sup>; N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>: sp<sup>2</sup>; N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>: sp<sup>3</sup>.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-08}
### Question 8 · 3.1 SQ Medium Q3(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> This question is about the structure and reactions of organic compounds. Fig. 3.1 shows the displayed formula of a type of fuel known as gasoline.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> State the IUPAC name of gasoline.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Give the general formula for the homologous series to which gasoline belongs.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> The gasoline shown in Fig. 3.1 can react with chlorine in the presence of UV light to form various chlorinated products.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> State the type of organic mechanism used in this reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Draw the skeletal formula of the four monochlorinated isomers formed.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(iii)</strong> State the type of isomerism shown by the isomers in (b)(ii).</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> There are two possible reactions of 1-bromopropane with sodium hydroxide. State the role of the aqueous hydroxide ion, name compound X, and give the conditions and mechanism for the alternative reaction forming propene.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Pentanal reacts with hydrogen cyanide ions to form 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> In terms of orbitals and bonding, explain why the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> State the shape and bond angle adopted by the carbonyl carbon after reaction with hydrogen cyanide.</p>
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/13/rebuilt/sq-medium-q3c-nucleophilic-substitution.png" class="question-figure" alt="Hydroxide ion attacking 1-bromopropane to form compound X and bromide ion">
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Gasoline is an alkane; give the name and formula shown in Fig. 3.1.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Free-radical substitution; the four products are positional isomers.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> OH<sup>−</sup> is a nucleophile; X is propan-1-ol; hot ethanolic hydroxide gives elimination.</li><li><strong>(d)(i)</strong> The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised with three regions of electron density, giving trigonal-planar geometry.</li><li><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> After CN<sup>−</sup> addition it is sp<sup>3</sup>, tetrahedral, with an angle close to 109.5°.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-09}
### Question 9 · 3.1 SQ Medium Q4(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Name the shortest straight-chain alkane to have structural isomers and the isomer.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> State the type of isomerism shown by the isomers in part (a)(i).</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> exists as several isomers. Name the homologous series that C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> belongs to.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Draw the skeletal formulae of two cyclic C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> isomers and two C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> isomers that show cis/trans isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(iii)</strong> There are two unsaturated C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> isomers that do not show cis/trans isomerism. Name these isomers and explain why they do not show cis/trans isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Draw the displayed formulae of 2,4-dimethylhexan-3-ol, 2,4-dimethyl-3-chloropentane and 2-aminobutane and, where appropriate, identify any chiral centres.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> 1-bromopropan-1-ol exhibits optical isomerism. Draw 3D representations of the two enantiomers.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Butane and 2-methylpropane; chain isomerism.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Alkene; cyclic examples include cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane; cis/trans examples include cis- and trans-but-2-ene; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not show cis/trans because one alkene carbon has two identical groups.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Draw all three displayed formulae and mark each carbon attached to four different groups.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> Draw the two non-superimposable mirror-image structures.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #aso-sq-10}
### Question 10 · 3.1 SQ Medium Q5(a-d)

<p><strong>(a)</strong> Explain why cyclohexane C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> has a puckered, non-planar shape by making reference to the C–C–C bond angles and the type of hybridisation of carbon in the molecule.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Urea, CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, is present in solution in animal urine. Describe the hybridisation of C and N in the molecule, giving approximate bond angles.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Describe the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane and explain how the concept of hybridisation can be used to explain the shape of the methane molecule.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> A molecule of ethanol is shown in Fig. 5.1. Deduce the hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in the diagram.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Carbon is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised and prefers 109.5°. A planar hexagon would force 120°, so the ring puckers.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> The carbonyl C is sp<sup>2</sup> with angles near 120°; the N atoms are approximately sp<sup>2</sup> because their lone pairs are delocalised.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Carbon forms four equivalent sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals directed tetrahedrally, giving 109.5° H–C–H angles.</li><li><strong>(d)</strong> The marked carbon is classified from its number of electron-density regions; a carbon in a single-bonded saturated environment is sp<sup>3</sup>.</li></ul></details>
:::
